rounds.proof_sketch: For float32 input: scalar_t=float, VEC_SIZE=4. The else branch (lines 72-75) is taken since constexpr condition is false. Variable 'result' has type 'scalar_t' which IS 'float'. Original: static_cast<float>(float) → float. Mutant: float → float. Both are identical assignments to float_out[i]. The cast float→float is a no-op identity operation.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation removes a static_cast<float>(result) where 'result' is already of type float (since scalar_t=float for the float32 kernel path). In C++, casting a float to float is an identity operation that produces bit-identical results. The mutation cannot be distinguished because both expressions yield exactly the same float value for any input. This is true regardless of the numerical values in the tensor - whether near-zero, denormals, NaN, Inf, or any other float value, the cast from float to float never changes any bits.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable. The mutation removes a redundant type cast that has no semantic effect. When scalar_t=float (the only dtype tested per input specification), static_cast<float>(result) where result is already float is a no-op. No value-level test can distinguish the original from the mutant because they produce bit-identical results for all float32 inputs.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing tools should include static analysis to detect and exclude semantically-equivalent mutations such as redundant casts (casting T to T). This would reduce false-positive surviving mutants and improve mutation score accuracy. Consider adding a 'redundant_cast' rule to the EMD Layer 1 static rules that detects static_cast<T>(expr) where expr already has type T.
